Photograph: VCG/Getty Images China China denounces US threat of sanctions over trade with Iran Beijing says it will take ‘all necessary measures’ to protect its interests as US steps up efforts to isolate Tehran Explainer: could US sanctions threaten China-Iran ties? Julian Borger Senior international correspondent Tue 25 Aug 2026 07.43 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google China has denounced the threat of US sanctions for its trade with Iran , saying any such measures would be illegal, and warned it would take “all necessary measures” to protect its national interests. Beijing’s rejection of the US threat of secondary sanctions for any country or entity continuing to trade with Tehran had been predicted. China buys an estimated 80% of Iran’s oil exports and it has defied previous US efforts to limit the flow of revenue to the Tehran regime. Its statement of opposition raises the question of how far the Trump administration would be prepared to go in confronting China and its financial system in the drive to isolate Iran . In making the sanctions threat on Monday, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced an initial set of sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels for alleged involvement in trade with Iran, but there were no Chinese financial institutions on the list, despite their involvement in financing the Iranian oil trade. The omission reflected US caution. China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil. Could US sanctions threaten those ties? Read more Asked why the Trump administration had not declared immediate sanctions and had stopped short of naming potential sanctions targets, Bessent replied: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Financial and trade experts say the administration is well aware of the risk of Chinese retaliation before a scheduled summit next month between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. China could strike back through financial markets or with limits on its export of critical minerals. The spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry, Lin Jian, told reporters on Tuesday: “Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted. “China has already stated many times that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions. China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests.” Iran has been economically wrecked by the war and the accompanying US blockade, but it maintained its defiance in response to Bessent’s threats of total isolation. The economy minister, Ali Madanizadeh, said on state television: “Our defence is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack.” An oil tanker was reportedly hit on Tuesday by an unidentified projectile at the mouth of the strait of Hormuz. Only two commercial vessels were reported to have successfully made the transit through the narrow waterway on Monday. The declaration of what Bessent called Operation Economic Outcast suggests that the prospects of a resolution to the conflict with Iran are still remote. It also suggests a lean towards economic measures and away from military force after a six-month war that has not brought about the intended Iranian capitulation. The near closure of the strait of Hormuz and knock-on effect on oil prices and the global economy is a political risk for Trump as congressional elections loom in November. View image in fullscreen Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Beijing in May. They are due to meet again next month. Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty Images The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, insisted that further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using ‌kinetic strikes anywhere in the ​strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth ⁠told reporters on Monday. Bessent called the sanctions campaign unprecedented and compared it to the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” he said. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.” He said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances. “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.” Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of elections Read more Bessent said Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart. Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.” In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions. Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. But while sanctions can be effective, it is highly unlikely they will produce a quick settlement favourable to the United States.” Explore more on these topics China US foreign policy Iran US-Israel war on Iran Asia Pacific Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story China arrests US academic at conference for ‘espionage activities’ Same but different: how Xi and China welcomed Trump and Putin What was actually achieved at Trump and Xi’s ‘stalemate summit’ in Beijing? https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0r.text: Image source, Kazakh Ministry of Defence/Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, The investigation is looking into decision-making by senior military officials By Paulin Kola Published 52 minutes ago Five senior military officials have been detained in Kazakhstan following the death of 14 service members who were taking part in military exercises. Those who died were among a total of 17 who were swept into the Caspian Sea as they were disembarking from a boat on Thursday. Officials say the incident occurred "during a combat training mission due to a sharp deterioration in meteorological conditions and increasing winds". Three were rescued. Those detained include the chief of staff and first deputy commander of Kazakhstan's Naval Forces, two military unit commanders, and the commanders of a marine company and a boat. They are suspected of criminal negligence. An interior ministry committee has been set up to investigate the incident, which occurred some 43km (27 miles) from the city of Aktau in south-western Kazakstan. Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said a pretrial investigation into the deaths was being conducted. The investigation was looking into the decisions made during the organisation and execution of the military training exercise, whether safety requirements had been observed, and weather conditions had been taken into account - in addition to technical specifications of the boat. More than 500 military personnel, warships and coastal units were participating in the Caspian Defense 2026 military exercise, according to the Kazakh ministry of defence. Photograph: Armin Durgut/AP First Edition newsletter Serbia Friday briefing: How a leaderless student group is challenging power in Serbia In today’s newsletter: ​Born from the fury surrounding the deadly Novi Sad station collapse, Serbia’s Student List has taken its protests all the way to the elections in an unprecedented grassroots campaign Libby Brooks Fri 23 Oct 2026 01.43 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 01.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. As waves of youth-led protests swell across Europe , prompted by the cost of living, unaffordable housing and education standards, in Serbia the younger generation is taking on the apparatus of the state itself. In tight-run parliamentary elections this Sunday, the country’s most consequential political movement in decades, Student List, is challenging former Slobodan Milošević henchman Aleksandar Vučić and his 12-year domination of Serbian politics. Two years on from a singular national tragedy that galvanised public anger at state cover-ups and corruption, gen Z have channelled their energy and fury into a bold experiment in direct democracy, creating a genuinely leaderless, grassroots movement that is firing up disaffected voters across the country. I spoke to Julian Borger , our senior international correspondent, who has just returned from Belgrade, about their hopes of emulating the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary and the potential for a democratic domino through central Europe. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Ukraine | Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations. UK politics | Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader. Europe news | Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years. Energy | Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen. In depth: ‘The essence of our movement is direct democracy’ View image in fullscreen A large group of Student List supporters arrive in Belgrade after marching from several cities across Serbia. Photograph: Pierre Crom/Getty Images It was, one Serbian student told me, “the drop that overflowed the glass”. On 1 November 2024, the collapse of a concrete canopy at the railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second largest city, killed 16 people. The youngest was a six-year-old girl, Sara Firic, who was sitting on a bench with her grandfather and older sister. The Serbian Times reported they were still holding hands when their bodies were dug out of the rubble. In the aftermath of the disaster, student-led protests developed organically, with demonstrators blocking a nearby crossroads for the same number of minutes as lives lost. As details emerged of botched refurbishment work carried out in what critics described as a corrupt deal with a Chinese consortium, the anger mounted. Ongoing protests were brutally suppressed and Vučić himself branded demonstrators western-backed “terrorists”. Two years later, that single tragedy has sparked a mass movement for accountability and inclusive democracy to counter the creeping authoritarianism of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS). “There was a deep well of public discontent, and the students were inspirational in keeping the protest movement going,” says Julian. Vučić expected the protesters to dissipate – instead, the mounting pressure forced the president to resign and call a snap parliamentary election, as he endeavours to consolidate his 12 years in power in a Putin-inspired switch to become prime minister. In response, the student movement is fielding a list of 250 candidates of its own, mainly locally respected academics but also actors, musicians and farmers, with each candidate approved by citizens’ assembly. Some polling suggests that Student List is edging ahead; others that the SNS is consolidating support. Julian tells me he left Belgrade with the sense that anything could happen on Sunday. How did a student network put together an election campaign? The Serbian student I spoke to is buzzing ahead of Sunday’s vote: “We’re really excited,” he tells me over the phone from the Serbian capital. “We hope we win.” He is studying for a masters in dramatic arts at the University of Belgrade, and asks not to be named in accordance with the leader-less structure of his movement. He talks me through the “big collective effort”, including collecting canvas data door to door, and the “A student in every village” programme targeting Vučić’s base of rural voters, all coordinated by democratic citizens’ assembly. The thinking is that a higher turnout of disaffected voters will favour Student List. Julian encapsulates the Student List movement as “a bold democratic experiment”, and that is how my student describes it: “The essence of our movement is direct democracy. This collective effort is about making people feel part of the decision-making, not just spectators.” When Julian joined Student List volunteers canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb, they were met with overwhelmingly positive reactions – “the response was ‘bring it on’” – though he caveats that opinion in outlying suburbs varies from those of the urban intelligentsia and others in more rural settings. “People were saying to the volunteers, ‘Take my contact and tell me anything I can do on election day.’ There’s a feeling of now or never.” The demands of the student movement are focused on governance, Julian tells me, and their slogan, “Serbia or mafia?”, highlights repeated allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, something the government denies. “Student List wants a rules-based order that conforms with the constitution on paper, not the system of classic crony capitalism that Vučić has established, where everything depends on your link to the SNS.” How has the Vučić regime fought back? Julian says Vučić is plainly taking the Student List threat seriously. He made 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total. But the elections are happening in a context of growing repression: Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years. And only last week, the Guardian revealed that Vučić intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected landmark in Belgrade for a Trump tower, another spur for recent protests. A September survey for Serbian pro-democracy group the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) found no negative coverage of the ruling majority on the country’s television channels, compared with 37% of the time for the opposition. Student List has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping overseas polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to Julian’s request to comment. Meanwhile the digital rights group SHARE Foundation found that members of the student movement had been targeted by advanced spyware, while Reuters this week reported on intimidation and beating of protesters by police. What is the likely aftermath of Sunday’s elections? With preliminary results expected in the early hours of Monday morning, a fundamental problem for the country is that neither side sees the other as legitimate, says Julian. “So in the aftermath of the election, barring a really clear decision, it will be disputed one way or another.” Indeed, the European Council on Foreign Relations has warned of further street protests and possible violent repression, depending on the outcome and the margin of victory. Big questions remain around how Student List would configure themselves as a government. Reforming the state and economy after more than a decade of highly centralised SNS control will be immensely challenging. So far their policy platform has been decided by full general assembly, and divisive issues such as future relations with Kosovo or Russia, and stance on EU membership, have been played down. Although Serbia is an EU-candidate country, public opinion on accession is split, and the SNS has counter-balanced relationships with the US, Russia and China, particularly after the Trump administration opened dialogue on energy and technology with them earlier this year. A Student List win would throw this geopolitical balancing act, which protesters argue brings little benefit to the people of Serbia, up in the air and potentially bring the country closer to Europe. And a contested Vučić victory would challenge the EU on whether to freeze diplomacy and funding to the country. The student organiser I spoke with is clear that regime change is just the beginning: “Once we remove the regime, the big debate starts in Serbia about what we should do next. Should we join the EU? What about foreign policy? How are we going to democratise the country? There’s a lot that’s not working because of corruption. But right now we’re focused on these elections.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen Central High School’s desegregated prom, 1967. Photograph: Jamie Lee Taete Monroe County detention centre, Florida is an unlikely, but successful, place for a zoo. Beginning as a makeshift rescue centre for some local ducks in 1994, the prison now houses animals such as a partially blind ostrich and a capybara. Select prisoners look after the animals and their enclosure alongside the more mundane chores inside the prison. Research shows working with animals helps improve mental health and decreases the likelihood for prisoners to reoffend. Zoo supervisor Jeanne Selander, and former prisoners, have much to say on the positive effects the Zoo has brought to the prison and its wider community. Photograph: Getty Images Ukraine Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years The Ukrainian president called the US decision strong, but added that delivery of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠could take years Guardian staff and agencies Fri 30 Oct 2026 22.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. “The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday. The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine. Zelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’ Read more Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors. “Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.” Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves ⁠of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles. On Thursday, a Russian drone ​strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform ‌in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five ‌died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said. Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners. He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”. Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington ⁠after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries. But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s. One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring ‌forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors. Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, ​along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement. The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors. The US has ⁠supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, ​raising concerns about inventories of key air defense ​and precision-guided weapons.
